en: "A carbine bullet will not cut it,"
She had written in a note at its collar.
She had given that coat itself
The name "Badana."
Badana, which no bullet pierced—
Semetey strode proudly,
Showing that he was a hero,
And dressed Külchoro in it.
Again there was a wondrous object;
At the pommel of his saddle,
Level with his navel,
Your blood-taking prince fastened on him
The weapon called Kabyrga.
The iron no bullet pierced,
The armor fashioned separately,
Over Külchoro's kidney
He placed the iron again.
There was a coat made as a short jacket;
Its lower edge reached
Only to his navel
When he put that coat on.
Letting its skirt fall upward,
He dressed in the bulletproof coat;
When told he was going to Toltoy,
Without a frown or knitted brow,
The boy laughed openly in joy,
Proudly dressing in
The splendid coat no bullet pierced.
When told he was going to Kozho,
Without a frown or knitted brow,
Without stirring or grieving,
He smiled openly in joy.
Semetey, the prince's son,
Revealing his princely nature,
Dressed the boy in at least
Twelve kinds of splendid things
No common mortal wore,
So that Choro, son of Almambet,
Would not be struck by a stray bullet,
And death would not reach him in vain.
Buttoning up his whole body,
Armoring every rounded surface
With blue iron,
The young prince Semetey
Showed his heroism
And dressed Külchoro
In every kind of battle gear,
Then stood grieving, downcast.
The Gray Purse left as a gift
By Manas, gone to Judgment Day,
He had Külchoro gird around himself;
Then the bold young lad—
To think of him made the heart burn.
He dressed Külchoro
In Akolpok left by Manas.
When blood-taking Manas lived,
The road on which he struck Kalday had closed;
Unable to keep looking at the boy,
The only son of Manas
Felt smoke sting his nostrils.
Your hero, called a warrior prince,
Looked upon the boy;
His black eyes, like a saker falcon's,
Filled with tears without blinking.
He raged and groaned,
Smoke stinging his nostrils;
The leopard, son of Manas,
Broke down and wept aloud:
"He was only a boy of twelve,
A soul still learning to think.
He has not yet reached fifteen;
The taste of Kanykey's breast milk
Has not yet left his palate.
His shoulder bones have not yet hardened;
His time has not yet come
To match himself against Toltoy of the Zhediger.
His ribs have not yet filled out;
His time has not yet come
To grapple with Toltoy of the Zhediger."
For the boy who had never seen an enemy,
When he rode toward the foe,
A heavy rule fell upon his thoughts.
Your tiger could not bear to watch.
When the blessed boy slung it on,
It was the mirror of his moonlike shoulder;
When sent against a clashing enemy,
It was the solace of his entrusted soul.
When wielded in play, it killed;
When wielded in earnest, it slaughtered.
No one struck by its bullet escaped capture;
No one who toyed with it escaped alive.
The Almabash of surpassing steel,
Which would not fail for sixty days—
He now hung Akelte, left by Manas,
Upon Külchoro.
It struck whatever met its wrath;
Yesterday, in the desert of Mediyan,
It was found upon the open plain,
One of six blades fallen from heaven,
Well suited for striking the foe,
The strongest of sword blades:
When drawn in anger,
It never went without drinking blood;
Unless it drank its fill of blood,
It would not return to its sheath.
The fitting heirloom from his father
He proudly gave to the boy.
Semetey's battle-axe—
The master smith Bölökbay
Had joined and drawn out its point.
If an enemy came charging,
When swung in anger,
It lengthened to a fathom;
When about to strike the foe,
It glowed red like fire.
The battle-axe was a proud weapon,
Worthy of noble Semetey.
Hammered and polished underneath,
Master smith Bölökbay
Had made it through great toil.
If you ask about Bölökbay,
A star in the heavens had turned gray;
Dөөтү and Bölökbay
Had become friends twelve times.
While he was making the axe,
Unable to withstand the demands of his bellows,
Many young bulls were slaughtered;
Unable to meet its need for charcoal,
Many forests were destroyed.
The master of masters had forged it,
Wrapping its handle in gold,
Drawing its steel edge razor-sharp;
It felled anyone who attacked.
If he met Toltoy of the Zhediger
Out on the deserted plain,
If they stood rein to rein
And fought with battle-axes,
"Let its purpose strike home then;
Let him enter with the battle-axe."
He now beheld the boy's fierce spirit.
With deliberate instructions,
He now gave him the battle-axe.
If they stood rein to rein
And fought collar to collar,
He now gave the white Tinte
To hang around Külchoro's neck.
Looking nowhere around him,
Your ocean heaved in grief;
Sparing nothing for the boy,
He placed Syrnayza in his hand.
Showing his ocean-like greatness,
He had Külchoro mount
Mountain-like Buurul,
Standing saddled and ready.
When the boy mounted the horse,
Thirty young women and thirty maidens,
With Aychürök among them,
She voiced her sorrow, sobbing:
"Alas, Külchoro
Could have stayed here tonight!"
She cried out in regret.
When the boy mounted the horse,
Do not ask how the boy appeared.
Thirty young women and thirty maidens
Had nine black calves
Cut into pieces,
And offered them in sacrifice for the boy;
Sobbing as they performed the rite,
The thirty young women and thirty maidens—
"Amen!" they cried over the boy,
Sobbing as they gave their blessing.
Your poor sister-in-law Chürök
Had more worries than her heart could hold:
"May the boy remain safe."
Her tears ran in ten directions.
"The moon is dark, the night overcast—
What will this night become?
If Toltoy defeats him,
What will become of the days
Of this Chürök standing here?
His grip is hard as iron.
Do not let people say,
'Because of Aychürök's affliction,
She had her boy, a flame of fire,
Slaughtered.'
God, fulfill my prayer;
If you created him as a living soul,
God, keep her boy safe!
You have hung a battle-axe at your waist;
At twelve years of age,
You have set out upon a journey.
May a host support you on your journey;
O keen falcon, return blessed with good fortune.
May autumn cool your thoughts;
May it lay flat the enemy you seek.
Oh, my dear young falcon,
Spear a man on the downward slope;
Spear two in a row together.
Return safely, my tiger;
May your father, the leopard
Gone to the next world, be your companion."
Thirty young women and thirty maidens
Sobbing together,
With Aychürök among them,
Spread their hands and cried out.
Semetey, son of Manas—
Let me tell of the hero's condition.
Wrapped in the blue Kübө coat,
Straining like a blue tiger,
With a rope slung around his neck,
He led a white-gray mare
That had borne no foal for seven years.
The hero, son of Manas,
Slung the rope around his neck
And prayed to the Creator:
He spread his hands, saying, "Amen!"
His heart cruelly divided,
Tears pouring from his eyes,
He slung around his neck
The great purse left by Manas
And prayed to the one God:
"Amen, God, amen!
The one horse equal in worth to a life
Carries the young boy away.
If you let it be flattened, that is disgrace.
Buurul, whom none would give when asked—
When the boy mounted without inspiring envy,
My age was cruelly scorched.
He is riding away to witness
The suffering laid down by the Creator;
A young boy of twelve
Is riding away to die
At Toltoy of the Zhediger's hands.
Will practiced Chynkozho
Spear through and overturn
The twelve-year-old boy,
I lament before God,
And take Buurul beneath him as plunder?!
You have multiplied these worries so greatly;
Will the Almighty reveal
The boy, small as a crow?
My thoroughbred Narbuudan
Would not tire if ridden for six months.
I lament before God
For Külchoro, my kinsman.
The prayer of my kinsman—
Unable to remain standing, this poor soul—
I stand asking it of God.
May the blessing remain with the boy.
My time is cruelly divided;
If brave Toltoy is skillful,
It seems he will seize
The twelve-year-old boy.
Thinking of this, my wretched soul,
My time is cruelly divided.
The twelve-year-old boy—
